doc.title: Lew Soloff interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000

title: Electric music and the Rainforest rhythm section
summary: Volume problems in electric music, the star rhythm section for the Rainforest concert, and the intense rehearsals.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Tears of course was in a class by itself. You know how big that band was at the time. That was a real trip. We were the second biggest band in the world to the Beatles. But this band was very far removed from that kind of success, but way more successful than anything else I was with outside of BS&T. And this one was called MJQ. They call it MJQ. So maybe if I change my name from Lew Soloff’s Food Group to LSFD maybe something will happen. Yeah, maybe some initials, maybe that’ll do it. Anyway just to let you know where my head is at with music, I like to improvise in many contexts. I like to play straight ahead jazz but I also just as much like to play more of a world beat, narrow music in a way, which is kind of funk-fusion, R&B branched, in other words there’s a whole area of music, and some is finally being creative, that has some of the complexity and intricacies and depth — that’s the word I’m looking for — of the straight ahead music. The hard thing about the music based on some kind of electric instruments is that often times volume is a negative factor. Because if the volume is so high that you have to play loud all the time to be heard, it’s very hard to think creatively. Because part of music is having that dynamic thing from five p’s to five f’s, and being able to use them with it have the whole band come down and up because they can hear you. But if an electric rhythm section is playing, except in very few hands, these things can’t happen. Because the instrument control over the volume is not there as much as the others. And I think that’s one of the biggest problems with that. But talk about an intense groove? Whew. You should have heard that band behind the R&B acts. There were two guitarists, there was Steve Cropper and Nile Rogers. And Steve Cropper invented a lot of that stuff and Nile Rogers is fabulous. The bass player was Nathan East. The drummer was Narada Michael Walden, and the — I can’t pronounce his name right, Greg Phillinganes was the piano player. Also Leon Pendarvis was a piano player and a guy named Frank — I can’t remember his last name right now because I just met him. And it was an astounding rhythm section. Astounding. And there was a great percussionist there too.
How much time did you have to get this whole thing together?

We rehearsed — by the way, you never saw such intensity in musicians. Everybody was working for basically the Rain Forest Charity. It was either a nice nominal payment, but not considering the hours, but it was a nice nominal payment. It was a generous nominal payment, or else twice this payment was offered in value of tickets and things like that. And high-fallutin dinners and stuff like that. But even though many people donated their services totally, and took just the ticket and the dinner, many people did that, I never saw anything like it. We rehearsed for 13 hours straight the first day. There was maybe a half hour to 45 minutes taken for lunch; a half hour to 45 minutes taken for dinner. But outside of that there wasn’t any breaks during the day at all. And the next day we did ten and a half hours.
